Guy de Maupassant. The French short-story master and novelist whose work epitomised the aesthetic and moral clarity of late-nineteenth-century realism.

A protégé of Gustave Flaubert, Maupassant brought surgical precision to tales of provincial France, military life, and the human heart. He never sentimentalised, always observing. His hundreds of stories, published at a prolific rate, established the short form as a vehicle for complete psychological and social portraiture. His influence on the genre is arguably greater than any writer's except Chekhov.

His signature stories endure across centuries. "The Necklace" tells of a woman who borrows a diamond necklace, loses it, and spends a decade repaying what turns out to be costume jewellery—a meditation on class and self-deception. "A Piece of String" shows a peasant picking up a string on the road, suspected of theft, his reputation destroyed by a misunderstanding he cannot correct. "The Horla" is a psychological horror story told in diary form, descending into madness and paranoia. And "Balls of Fat" presents a prostitute who sacrifices her body for the survival of bourgeois passengers during the Franco-Prussian War.

Maupassant was a master of the plot twist and the ironic reversal. Stories that deliver a final sentence that reframes everything before it. He was fascinated by the gap between appearance and reality. His characters are undone by misunderstanding, vanity, and circumstance. Published over three hundred stories in his lifetime, each precise and complete—an industrial feat of craft.

He arrived as Flaubert's heir to French realism at precisely the moment when naturalism was challenging romanticism. He negotiated both. His precision was Flaubertian, but his subject matter—the petit bourgeoisie, soldiers, peasants—was Zolaist. What set him apart was his fundamental pessimism and his irony. Maupassant never lets his characters off the hook with sentiment. A woman's descent into poverty, a soldier's dehumanisation, a workman's irreversible loss—these are treated with cool detachment that somehow becomes deeply moral. In quiz bowl, Maupassant is essential to questions about nineteenth-century European realism, the short story's formal properties, and irony as a structural principle.
